title: The Nativity of Mary (8 September)
hook: nine months after the Immaculate Conception, a birthday for Mary
tomorrow: The Exaltation of the Cross (14 September)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Assumption, Mary taken up. Your line was she went ahead. Whom did you picture on the road ahead of you? Day six hundred eighty.

Count back nine months from the eighth of September, and you land on the eighth of December. That's the Immaculate Conception, the feast of Mary's conception in her mother's womb. The Church's calendar does the arithmetic on purpose. So today is a birthday. In Malta it's a public holiday; in Italian towns and in parts of India there are processions and sweets. And the Gospel the Church reads for it is one that's easy to skip: the long list of names at the start of Matthew.
screen: `DECEMBER TO SEPTEMBER: NINE MONTHS.` → `A BIRTHDAY.` → `A LIST OF NAMES.`

segments.voice: Like her parents' names, Mary's birth isn't told in the Bible. The details again come from the Protoevangelium of James, and an old tradition places her birth in Jerusalem, near the pool of Bethesda, where a church of Saint Anne stands today. The feast began in the East, and Rome took it up later. So why read a genealogy on her birthday? Matthew counts it out as three sets of fourteen generations, from Abraham through David and the exile, and it's not all heroes. It includes a man who helped sell his brother, a king who arranged a soldier's death, and women with complicated stories, Tamar, Rahab, Ruth, and the wife of Urias. Generation after generation of ordinary, mixed-up people. And then the list breaks its own pattern. Line after line, it's been so-and-so begot so-and-so. At the end, in the Douay-Rheims: "And Jacob begot Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ." The rhythm stops at her. Mary's birthday is the Church saying: here is the place where the long, crooked family line was heading. One ordinary-looking girl, born, tradition says, to an older couple, in a city full of pilgrims. Catholics greet her today, often with the angel's own words from Luke: "Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee: blessed art thou among women." There's no cake in the liturgy. But in some towns, there is cake.
screen: `NOT IN THE BIBLE; A TRADITION.` · `THREE SETS OF FOURTEEN.` · `NOT ALL HEROES.` · `THE RHYTHM STOPS AT HER.` · then, large: `OF WHOM WAS BORN JESUS, WHO IS CALLED CHRIST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wish Mary a happy birthday. It's a simple, almost childlike thing, and that's the point. Sit, and think about the people who were part of the line that led to you: names you know, names you don't. Then, if you pray, greet Mary the way Catholics do, with the angel's words, Hail, full of grace, and wish her a happy birthday. If you don't pray, think of a birthday you've forgotten lately, and plan to honor it. The bell holds the time.
The Nativity of Mary. Mary's birthday, the eighth of September, nine months after the Immaculate Conception. Today's word.
Your line: her birthday. Today, find out one name from your own family line that you didn't know, a great-grandparent or further back. Day six hundred eighty.

howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin Mary on 8 September, nine months after the Immaculate Conception; the Gospel is Matthew's genealogy, and in places such as Malta and parts of Italy and India the day is marked with processions and festivals.

notes: Feast origin: likely Jerusalem, 5th–6th century; adopted in Rome in the 7th century (under Pope Sergius I). Confirm.
Tradition of Mary's birth near the pool of Bethesda (Church of Saint Anne, Jerusalem); a rival tradition places it in Nazareth or Sepphoris.
Genealogy: Matthew counts three sets of fourteen (forty-two generations); the actual names listed differ slightly. 'Forty lines' is approximate.
Douay-Rheims spells 'Urias' for Uriah; script uses that.
'A man who sold his brother' refers to Judah (Genesis 37:26–27), who is in the line; confirm. 'A king who arranged a soldier's death' is David.
Festivities in Malta (Victory Day) and Goa/India (Monti Fest); confirm.

Editor review (2026-10-01): 'forty-two generations' and 'forty lines' replaced with Matthew's own count (1:17, three sets of fourteen); feast-origin centuries cut; Judah 'helped sell' his brother; 'one of only three births' cut from the word (day 674 already teaches it); 'most people skip' softened.
